Eight retaining-wall pathways Start with geometry, loads, water and access; then compare systems that can answer those facts. 01 Concrete Sleeper Retaining Walls Post-and-panel systems for straight or stepped residential walls where embedment, handling access, transitions, loads and drainage are designed as one scope. 02 Segmental Block & Masonry Retaining Walls Segmental and reinforced masonry options assessed against wall geometry, footing or reinforced-soil requirements, available footprint and finish. 03 Sandstone & Natural Stone Retaining Walls For a sloping garden or failing older terrace, stone may offer a durable gravity solution when the site has sound bearing, enough footprint and safe machinery access. 04 Timber Sleeper & Garden Retaining Walls Treated timber options for appropriate lower terraces, considered alongside member durability, moisture exposure, fixings, drainage and future replacement needs. 05 Gabion Retaining Walls Rock-filled basket walls for sites where their footprint and appearance fit, with foundation, basket, stone and filter details clearly specified. 06 Retaining Wall Drainage & Excavation Coordination Planning the collection zone, separator, subsoil drain, outlet, excavation access and spoil movement that sit behind a workable wall scope. 07 Engineered & Approval-Ready Retaining Walls A coordinated information, design and certification path for walls outside simple exemptions or affected by significant loads, boundaries or nearby structures. 08 Retaining Wall Repairs & Replacement Cause-led assessment of movement, decay, washout and cracking followed by a clear repair, stabilisation or replacement scope. Read the section The wall face is not the whole level change Canberra blocks range from established inner-south gardens to recent Molonglo cut-and-fill sites. In both settings, a wall interacts with the land above it, any building or driveway load, the boundary, and water moving through or over the soil. Take one wide photograph from each end, then record the maximum retained height and the broader change in ground level. Add close views of lean, cracking, decay, washout or persistent wetness only after the overall geometry is visible. Canberra keeps producing three versions of the same job Canberra was built outward in waves, and each wave met the terrain differently. The inner south around Red Hill, Forrest and Griffith was laid out across established slopes, and its walls now sit inside gardens that have had eighty years to mature over them. The Weston Creek, Belconnen and Tuggeranong expansions cut house benches into hillsides below Oakey Hill, Cooleman Ridge and Mount Taylor. Gungahlin from the 1990s, then the Molonglo Valley suburbs after it, were formed by large-scale civil earthworks, so the levels on those blocks were inherited rather than chosen. That history is why almost every enquiry falls into one of three shapes. The first is a wall built to hold a house bench forty or fifty years ago that has reached the end of its service life, where the question is whether the structure is tired or the ground has changed. The second is a sound wall overtaken by later landscaping: a redirected downpipe, new paving, a raised garden bed or an irrigation line now feeds more water into the retained soil than the original drainage was ever built to release. The third is a newer estate boundary where the wall is part of the subdivision earthworks and any change has to work around levels, easements and a neighbour's ground. The local climate pushes on all three. Frosty winters, dry spells and short intense storm bursts mean retained ground here is repeatedly wetted and dried rather than held at a steady moisture. Walls fail slowly under that cycle, which is why a wall can look unchanged for years and then move noticeably in a single season. The order the decisions actually go in Work from the ground outwards. Establish what is being retained and what sits on top of it, then how water reaches and leaves that zone, then what can physically get to the wall, then what the ACT approval pathway requires, and only then which system to build. Reversing that order is what produces a wall that is well made and wrong for the site. Most of this you can record yourself in an afternoon with a tape, a phone and a walk around after rain. None of it makes you the engineer. It does mean the first person who looks at the wall is answering the real question rather than guessing at it, and it means two written responses can be compared on the same set of facts.
